subject: english-literature
topicDisplay: Paper 1: Exploring Modern and Literary Heritage Texts
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: How long is the OCR GCSE English Literature Paper 1 (Exploring Modern and Literary Heritage Texts), and what proportion of the GCSE is it worth?
options: 1 hour 45 minutes, 64 marks, 40% of the GCSE
2 hours 15 minutes, 96 marks, 60% of the GCSE
questions.explain: OCR Component 01 is a 2-hour, 80-mark closed-text paper worth 50% of the qualification.

questions.q: Which two sections make up OCR Paper 1?
options: Section A: Poetry; Section B: Unseen poetry
Section A: Shakespeare; Section B: Modern drama
Section A: Modern prose or drama; Section B: 19th-century prose
Section A: 19th-century poetry; Section B: Modern prose
questions.explain: Paper 1 divides into Section A (modern prose or drama) and Section B (19th-century prose).

questions.q: Which of the following best states Assessment Objective 2 (AO2)?
options: Read, understand and respond to texts, using textual references
Analyse the language, form and structure used by a writer to create meanings and effects, using relevant subject terminology
Show understanding of the relationships between texts and the contexts in which they were written
Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures with accurate spelling and punctuation
questions.explain: AO2 rewards analysis of a writer's methods (language, form and structure) using apt terminology.

questions.q: Who wrote the modern drama set text 'An Inspector Calls'?
questions.explain: 'An Inspector Calls' was written by J.B. Priestley and first performed in 1945.

questions.q: George Orwell's 'Animal Farm' is best understood as an allegory of which historical event?
options: The Russian Revolution and its aftermath
questions.explain: 'Animal Farm' is a political allegory of the 1917 Russian Revolution and the rise of Stalinism.

questions.q: Who is the author of the 19th-century prose set text 'Frankenstein'?
questions.explain: Mary Shelley wrote 'Frankenstein', first published in 1818.

questions.q: Which author wrote the 19th-century novel 'Great Expectations'?
questions.explain: 'Great Expectations' was written by Charles Dickens and follows the growth of the orphan Pip.

options: A novel narrated entirely through letters
A novel tracing the psychological and moral growth of the protagonist from youth to adulthood
A poem lamenting the death of a person
A play performed without any scenery
questions.explain: A bildungsroman is a 'coming-of-age' novel charting a protagonist's development, as in 'Great Expectations'.

questions.q: Priestley sets 'An Inspector Calls' in 1912 but wrote it in 1945. Mr Birling's confident claims (e.g. that the Titanic is 'unsinkable') mainly allow Priestley to use which technique?
questions.explain: The 1945 audience knows Birling's predictions are wrong, creating dramatic irony that undermines his authority.

questions.q: In Golding's 'Lord of the Flies', what does the conch shell most clearly symbolise?
questions.explain: The conch grants the right to speak and represents civilised order, whose collapse mirrors the boys' descent into savagery.

questions.q: In Ishiguro's 'Never Let Me Go', the donation programme is used chiefly to explore which idea?
options: What it means to be human and the inevitability of mortality
questions.explain: The clones' fate prompts readers to reflect on humanity, memory and the mortality all people share.

questions.q: A student explains how 'An Inspector Calls' reflects Edwardian class divisions and Priestley's post-war socialist beliefs. Which Assessment Objective does this MOST directly address?
questions.explain: Linking a text to the context in which it was written is exactly what AO3 rewards.

questions.q: In Stevenson's 'The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde', the relationship between the two title figures is used to explore which central idea?
options: The duality of human nature — that each person contains both good and evil
questions.explain: Jekyll and Hyde embody the Gothic theme of duality: the coexistence of good and evil within one person.

questions.q: 'Frankenstein' opens with Walton's letters, which then frame Victor's account. What is the main effect of this frame narrative?
options: It removes all suspense from the plot
It creates layers of narration that lend credibility and distance to a fantastical tale
It confirms the story is a factual autobiography
It prevents the reader from sympathising with any character
questions.explain: The nested narrators make an incredible story feel authentic while inviting the reader to weigh differing viewpoints.

questions.q: Which set of features is most characteristic of the Gothic genre found in several 19th-century set texts?
options: Cheerful settings, comedy and happy endings
Gloomy settings, the supernatural, mystery and a sense of horror or dread
Rural farming life and seasonal routines
questions.explain: Gothic writing relies on foreboding settings, the supernatural and an atmosphere of terror, seen in 'Frankenstein' and 'Jekyll and Hyde'.

questions.q: Why might a novelist choose a first-person narrator, as in 'Great Expectations' or 'Never Let Me Go'?
options: To guarantee a completely objective account of events
To create intimacy and access to the narrator's thoughts, though the view may be limited or unreliable
questions.explain: First-person narration draws readers close to the narrator's perspective while reminding us it may be partial or biased.

questions.q: Read this invented line: 'As Pip trembled with fear, the marsh mist thickened and the wind howled across the graveyard.' Matching the weather to the character's emotion is an example of which technique?
questions.explain: Pathetic fallacy gives the natural world emotions that mirror a character's inner state to build atmosphere.

questions.q: Which quotation would best support an essay point about social responsibility in 'An Inspector Calls'?
options: 'a man has to mind his own business and look after himself'
'We don't live alone. We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other.'
'I gather there's a very good chance of a knighthood'
questions.explain: The Inspector's speech directly voices Priestley's message of collective social responsibility.

questions.q: A student writes: 'Priestley's metaphor "members of one body" fuses the family into a single image of shared duty.' Which Assessment Objective is the student mainly demonstrating?
questions.explain: Naming and analysing a writer's method (the metaphor) and its effect is the core of AO2.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) English Literature (J352) specification; Paper 1: Exploring Modern and Literary Heritage Texts
